#5256. Deutsche Bank Opens Digital Asset Custody to Paying Institutional Clients

Deutsche Bank opens up digital asset custody to paying institutional clients. The service includes storage, user experience improvements, and accessibility via the bank's own gateways. The bank announced the launch on November 11, as DB's official website reveals.

This is an improvement in the field of institutional adoption, even though it comes at a time when it might be unwarranted. The market is experiencing serious issues and constant outflows from both retail and institutional investors.

Surprisingly, the bank can provide both warm and cold storage options available directly through DB's infrastructure. According to the landing page, the platform will provide key storage via Hardware Security Modules. Access goes through Autobahn, the bank's own multi-channel gateway.

Compliance will also be handled by Deutsche Bank. Initially, the service will focus on core functions: custody of digital assets and transfers, with further capabilities planned.

The Asian market has yet to receive similar treatment. For now, the service is available in the EU, operating out of DB AG Frankfurt. An expansion to Asia is reportedly planned for 2027, though the details are yet to be confirmed.

Additionally, DB announced support for euro stablecoins such as EURC and EURAU, in addition to BTC, ETH, and USDC. This is an attempt to promote the adoption of EU-issued stablecoins as part of a strategy aimed at moving away from USDT dominance. EURAU is issued by AllUnity, a joint venture that includes DWS, the asset manager majority-owned by Deutsche Bank.

Self-custody or banks: that is the real question here. Industry experts such as Bloomberg's ETF analyst Eric Balchunas suggest that self-custody has been a worse option and that a custodian with funds protection and insurance is a better option for regular investors. Even Binance founder CZ admitted after the Ledger incident that self-custody comes with extra responsibilities.

Back in August, a Coldcard exploit drained 1,816 BTC from more than 5,000 cold-storage addresses, according to Fortune.

However, it puts some pressure on those who might receive their funds from grey sources. Unfortunately for them, a bank custodian creates another barrier, as every deposit has to go through the bank's compliance checks.

The altcoins are doing worse. Over seven days, Ethereum has lost 16.4%, Solana 14.7% and XRP 21.3%. CoinGecko values the whole crypto market at $2.42 trillion on Thursday, and Bitcoin makes up 60.5% of it.

Leverage made every drop bigger. More than $1 billion of bets were liquidated on Monday alone, almost all of them longs, the positions that profit only if prices rise. Liquidation means the exchange closes a trade by force once the trader’s collateral runs out, and those forced sales push the price down further.

So is this the flush that ends the crypto market slide, or is there more to come? The data has an answer, and it is not a comforting one.

The sell-off had no single cause. Four pieces of bad news landed one after another:

Each hit forced out more leveraged longs across the crypto market. Thursday’s slide continued the pattern on a smaller scale. We added up every forced closure in Bitcoin, Ether, Solana, XRP and Dogecoin futures on OKX, one of the largest exchanges, over the past 24 hours. Longs lost $27.6 million, against $12.3 million for shorts.

EXPLORE: Bitcoin Price Slides Toward $73K as Nvidia Plunges 9% and MSCI Drops Saylor’s Strategy

Big liquidations usually clear out the crowd. This time, the crowd came back.

In plain terms, traders keep buying every dip with borrowed money. That leaves fuel for another round of forced selling if Bitcoin drops through the next support. Bottoms tend to come when funding turns negative and open interest falls hard, a sign that leveraged buyers have given up.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Next Crypto to Hit 1 Dollar

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, which scores market mood from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed), reads 28 today. Fear is usually read as a buy signal. The history says it is not enough on its own.

We checked every day since February 2018 when the index sat at 28 or lower, 943 days in all, and where Bitcoin stood later.

This year’s two bottoms came with real panic. When Bitcoin hit $60,000 on February 6, the index read 9. When it bottomed at $57,800 on July 1, it read 11. Today’s 28 is fear, but it is not capitulation, the moment sellers give up all at once.

On the weekly chart, where each candle covers one week, Bitcoin has spent 2026 in a wide range. The low is $57,800 from July 1 and the high is $87,396 from late September. The midpoint is $72,598, almost exactly where Bitcoin trades now.

The price lost its 50-week exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $78,219. Its 200-week EMA sits at $69,597. Bitcoin closed below that line for 16 weeks this year, in February and March and again from June to mid-August, and both of the year’s bottoms formed during those stretches.

For the crypto market, three signs would say the bottom is close: the fear index dropping toward the teens, funding turning negative, and open interest falling as longs give up. None has shown up yet. Until they do, the 200-week EMA at $69,597 is the line that separates a pullback inside the 2026 range from a retest of the summer lows.

#5243. How to Build a Resilient Personal Investment Plan

Home » Op-ed » How to Build a Resilient Personal Investment Plan

Build a resilient personal investment plan with clear goals, diversified assets, and practical risk management. Learn how to assess costs, liquidity, and alternative investments before committing your money.

A sound investment plan ties your financial goals, time horizon, risk tolerance, and available resources together into one coherent strategy. Without that connection, even well-intentioned investment decisions can end up working against you. Diversification—spreading investments across and within asset classes rather than concentrating in a single holding—remains one of the most consistently cited principles in personal finance education. Some investors, while researching ways to diversify, come across physical assets such as gold bars as one example of exposure outside traditional stocks and bonds. This isn’t a recommendation; it’s simply an illustration of the kind of asset category investors may compare when evaluating a broader plan. This article focuses on the decision-making principles, risk management practices, and due diligence steps that apply regardless of which specific assets you ultimately choose.

Before selecting any investment, figure out what the money is actually for. Emergency savings, a short-term purchase, retirement, education funding, and long-term wealth building each come with different requirements for accessibility and acceptable volatility. Money you’ll need within the next year or two generally calls for safer, more liquid holdings. Money earmarked for goals decades away can typically absorb more fluctuation in exchange for growth potential.

It helps to separate two related but distinct concepts: risk tolerance, which is how much market fluctuation you can emotionally stomach, and risk capacity, which is your financial ability to absorb losses without jeopardizing your goals. Income stability, outstanding debt, the size of your emergency reserve, number of dependents, and investment time horizon all factor into risk capacity. Writing down your goals and constraints before researching specific investments helps prevent decisions driven by excitement or fear.

Several types of risk deserve separate attention: volatility (short-term price swings), permanent loss of capital, liquidity risk (difficulty converting an asset to cash without taking a discount), inflation risk (the erosion of purchasing power), and credit risk (a counterparty’s inability to meet its obligations).

Asset allocation refers to dividing a portfolio among categories such as stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, and alternative assets. Each category tends to respond differently to economic conditions, which is why diversification can reduce concentration risk—though it can’t eliminate the possibility of loss altogether. A realistic target allocation, one you can stick with through market stress rather than abandon at the first sign of volatility, matters more than a theoretically optimal one you can’t maintain. Rebalancing—periodically returning a portfolio to its intended mix—is a discipline rooted in preserving your chosen risk profile, not in predicting short-term market movements.

One educational approach organizes a portfolio into broad functions: liquidity for near-term needs, stability for capital preservation, growth for long-term objectives, and diversification for assets that may behave differently from your core holdings. This framework is illustrative only and shouldn’t be treated as a universal formula.

Key takeaway: A resilient portfolio begins with goals and constraints—not with chasing the latest fashionable investment.

Alternative assets are sometimes considered for diversification, potential inflation resilience, or reduced dependence on traditional financial assets. Gold, for instance, is occasionally discussed as a diversifier with no direct credit exposure, though its price can still fluctuate meaningfully. Historical behavior should never be mistaken for a guarantee of future performance.

Exposure to an asset like gold can take several forms: physical ownership, exchange-traded products, mining-company shares, or futures and other derivatives. Each form carries its own market, operational, counterparty, liquidity, and regulatory characteristics. Owning a physical asset is fundamentally different from owning a financial product whose value is merely linked to that asset’s price.

Understanding the economics of physical ownership requires a few plain-language definitions: the spot price is the current market price for immediate delivery; the purchase premium is the amount charged above spot price; the resale spread is the difference between what you pay and what you’d receive upon selling; storage and insurance costs are ongoing expenses tied to safekeeping; and liquidity describes how quickly and efficiently you can convert the asset back to cash.

Looking only at the quoted purchase price overlooks the full picture. The total cost of ownership includes premiums, storage, insurance, and eventual resale spreads. Before purchasing, it’s worth checking:

Be wary of unsolicited offers, urgency-based sales tactics, guaranteed-return claims, or requests for unusual payment methods. Compare multiple independent sources and hold on to receipts and ownership records. Product specifications, legal treatment, and tax rules vary by jurisdiction and change over time, so verify details through authoritative sources and qualified professionals.

Consider two hypothetical investors. The first spends time comparing dealers, calculates her total ownership costs, and limits her purchase to a small percentage of her portfolio in line with a written plan. The second, swayed by a high-pressure phone pitch promising rapid appreciation, commits a large sum without comparing alternatives or understanding the resale terms. The contrast says something about process quality, not about any specific asset.

Revisit your plan after major life changes—a new job, marriage, inheritance, retirement, or a significant shift in debt. Market movements alone don’t necessarily call for a strategic overhaul. Scheduled reviews should cover goal progress, emergency reserves, asset allocation, fees and ownership costs, and beneficiary or estate information. For decisions involving significant assets or complex obligations, consulting a qualified financial, tax, or legal professional is a wise move.

Before adding an alternative asset, consider:

A durable investment plan rests on clear objectives, genuine diversification, reasonable costs, adequate liquidity, and informed risk management—not on any single product. Physical precious metals may suit some financial plans, but they’re not automatically appropriate for every investor. Compare alternatives objectively, verify claims independently, and steer clear of decisions made under pressure. Take time to review your overall portfolio, write down the intended role of each holding, and seek qualified advice whenever a decision exceeds your own expertise.

#5240. Bitcoin Core Breaks Silence on Three Patched Security Vulnerabilities

Bitcoin Core developers have revealed three key security vulnerabilities, including a high-severity flaw that could potentially disrupt the mining capabilities of the Bitcoin network, preventing miners from creating new blocks.

As revealed in security advisories published on Nov. 10, the vulnerabilities impacted various elements of the Bitcoin Core software that powers many nodes underpinning the world's leading cryptocurrency.

One of the vulnerabilities, titled CVE-2025-62861, was rated as a high-severity issue due to its potential effect on Bitcoin miners.

The bug has the potential to create problems after a blockchain reorganization, which is when previously accepted blocks are replaced by the network with an alternative chain.

More precisely, the issue could cause an inconsistent state in the node's mempool, where all unconfirmed transactions are stored.

The vulnerability impacted Bitcoin Core software versions 28.0-28.2 and 29.0-29.1.

It was first reported on Sept. 26, 2025, by security researcher Niklas Goegge.

Beyond the mining vulnerability, Bitcoin Core developers have announced two further security problems, rated medium severity.

The first one (CVE-2025-62859) could enable malicious network participants to slow down Bitcoin block processing through an exploit that involves changes in transaction witness data.

Under some circumstances, it could make an affected node wait for up to 10 minutes before processing a block.

Moreover, such an attack could be repeated indefinitely on the node when the latter is running in specific configurations.

The vulnerability was found by Eugene Siegel in April 2025.

The second vulnerability (CVE-2025-62860) involved Bitcoin nodes that operate on the anonymous Tor network.

In fact, the Bitcoin Core developers revealed that thousands of reachable Bitcoin mainnet nodes had been granting permissions for incoming Tor connections.

Nevertheless, the issue did not affect nodes that do not use the optional whitelist configuration.

The three vulnerabilities are not new discoveries.

In fact, all of the issues were already fixed by the Bitcoin Core developers in October 2025.

The fixes were integrated into both Bitcoin Core 30.0, which was released on Oct. 10, and Bitcoin Core 29.2, rolled out on Oct. 14.

The high-severity mining vulnerability was also patched in Bitcoin Core 28.3.

The delay in the disclosure of the vulnerabilities was in line with the Bitcoin Core security policy, which usually calls for developers to wait at least two weeks after the end of life of the last affected software version before publishing details of medium- or high-severity vulnerabilities.

#5239. Why Is XRP Bleeding More Than Bitcoin, Ether, and Solana in November Sell-Off? Analyst Cites 3 Brutal Reasons

While Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana have also come under bearish pressure during November’s broader crypto market sell-off, XRP is taking a particularly brutal beating, leaving investors wondering why the token is underperforming its biggest rivals. According to prominent analyst EGRAG Crypto, the weakness is no coincidence, pointing to three key factors that could explain XRP’s sharper decline and signal why the token may continue struggling as bearish sentiment grips the market.

Crypto analyst EGRAG Crypto has highlighted XRP’s worsening performance against Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Solana (SOL) amid November’s broader cryptocurrency market drawdown. In a Nov. 10 post on X, the pundit noted the striking difference in losses since November 4, showing that Ripple’s XRP has suffered the steepest decline among the four major cryptocurrencies.

According to EGRAG Crypto’s figures, XRP has plunged 23.4% since November 4, significantly more than ETH’s 18.2% decline and SOL’s 17% drop. BTC has demonstrated greater resilience, losing just 10.4% over the same period.

The figures raise an important question: Why is XRP bleeding considerably more than its major competitors? EGRAG Crypto has pointed to three possible factors behind the token’s disproportionate weakness, offering a closer look at the selling pressure weighing on the Ripple-linked token.

The first factor is leveraged long liquidations, which EGRAG assigns a 30% probability. According to the analyst, forced liquidations of bullish positions, combined with weak buying demand, could be accelerating XRP’s fall. When leveraged traders are forced to close their positions during a downturn, the resulting selling pressure can trigger further losses and deepen an existing market correction.

The second possibility, which carries a 20% probability, is selling by early XRP holders. EGRAG suggests that longtime investors, often referred to as OGs, could be taking profits and rotating their capital into other cryptocurrencies. Such activity could increase selling pressure on XRP, particularly if large holders decide to reduce their exposure amid uncertain market conditions.

Finally, EGRAG assigns the highest probability, 50%, to what the expert describes as market manipulation or a deliberate liquidity hunt. Under this scenario, sharp price movements could be designed to trigger stop-loss orders and force weaker traders out of their positions before a potential recovery. The analyst believes this could explain why XRP is experiencing disproportionately heavy selling compared with other major cryptocurrencies.

Notably, these percentages represent EGRAG Crypto’s personal probability-based assessment rather than independently verified evidence of the causes behind XRP’s decline.

Beyond identifying the possible reasons behind XRP’s sharper decline, EGRAG Crypto has also highlighted several important price levels that could determine the token’s next move. The analyst identified the $1.00-$1.04 range as a critical stabilization zone, suggesting that holding this area could help XRP establish a floor amid the ongoing selling pressure.

On the upside, EGRAG believes bulls must first reclaim the $1.15 level before targeting $1.25. A recovery above these thresholds could signal improving buying momentum and offer some relief to investors after the recent losses.

Sharing a personal assessment, EGRAG Crypto said the ongoing price action appears more consistent with market manipulation designed to frighten newer investors into selling. However, the analyst raised a bigger question about whale activity, questioning whether deep-pocketed XRP holders are using the downturn to accumulate more tokens or adding to the selling pressure by offloading their holdings.

Ultimately, how whales respond to the current market weakness could offer important clues about XRP’s next direction. If large holders are absorbing the available supply, the sell-off could eventually lose momentum. Conversely, continued whale selling could make an already difficult recovery even harder for the sixth-largest cryptocurrency.

#5237. Ripple-Backed Evernorth Plunges 40% as Insiders Move to Sell 73.7 Million Shares

Ripple-backed XRP treasury company Evernorth Holdings (XRPN) is under extreme pressure as its shares have declined by over 40% while big investors like Ripple Labs move closer to potentially selling millions of shares.

Earlier this week, Evernorth filed a prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), indicating that the XRP-focused company has registered a whopping 73,688,162 Class A shares for potential resale by existing shareholders.

Evernorth's prospectus comes as the XRP-focused company is enduring a brutal stock market debut. XRPN began trading on Nasdaq on Oct. 12.

On Nov. 10, Evernorth's stock price dropped 23.54%. XRPN ended the day at $7.96, compared to $10.41 in the previous trading session. Moreover, about 1.39 million shares were traded, which is a significant jump from about 369,000 shares on Nov. 9.

So far, Evernorth's share price has declined by around 48% from its closing price on Oct. 28 ($15.26). The magnitude of the decline is even greater if we consider the high share price on its debut day ($19.39). XRPN's stock price is down by around 59% from that high.

Some of the biggest names and companies linked to the XRP ecosystem are shareholders who have registered shares for potential sale, as per the prospectus filed with the SEC.

For instance, the biggest shareholder is Arrington XRP Capital Fund, which was a sponsor of the merger between Evernorth and Armada Acquisition Corp. II. It has about 33.82 million shares registered for possible resale.

Similarly, the second-largest shareholder is Ripple Labs, which has about 18.14 million shares registered. Then there are various entities linked to SBI Holdings, a big Japanese financial institution. They have 11.79 million shares registered, as per the prospectus filed with the SEC.

The Larsen Lam Children's Remainder Trust, which is linked to Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen, has about 7.15 million shares registered for possible sale.

Other names mentioned in the filing include Pantera Capital, GSR Markets Switzerland and Kraken parent firm Payward.

It is important to understand that the fact that they've registered shares for sale doesn't mean that these investors have sold their holdings or necessarily plan to sell them.

For example, Ripple, the Arrington-sponsored entity and a Larsen-linked entity are all subject to six-month lock-up agreements following the completion of Evernorth's business combination on Oct. 9.

These lock-up agreements are typically set to expire on April 9, 2027, with some exceptions.

The appointment follows the launch of Phase’s Layer 1 blockchain mainnet and AI agent services, backed by $45 million in founder funding.

SAN FRANCISCO, November 11, 2026 — Phase, a technology company building the operating layer for the AI agent economy, today announced that Yana Prikhodchenko, former CEO of Cointelegraph, has joined the company as co-founder and CEO. She will lead strategy, global expansion and commercial development, working alongside founder Kirill Eves, as Phase scales its decentralized infrastructure for autonomous AI agents.

Prikhodchenko joins Phase after nearly five years at Cointelegraph, where she served as CEO, leading a global team of more than 200 people and transforming the company from a crypto news platform into a diversified group spanning media, marketing, research, acceleration and industry events. Before joining Cointelegraph, she spent more than a decade in senior leadership roles at major banking and insurance companies, including Allianz.

Phase is building the operating layer for the AI agent economy, giving AI agents everything they need to operate autonomously, from accessing the open web and orchestrating AI models to performing computing tasks and making payments. These services run on Phase’s Layer 1 blockchain, powered by a decentralized network of everyday devices whose owners earn rewards for validating transactions and contributing connectivity and computing power.

“AI agents are moving from answering questions to performing real tasks on our behalf, but the infrastructure they depend on was not built for autonomous systems. Phase is building an open, decentralized network that anyone can participate in. My focus is to bring this technology to developers and businesses worldwide and build the ecosystem needed to support the next generation of AI agents,” said Yana Prikhodchenko, co-founder and CEO of Phase.

“Yana brings extensive leadership experience across media, technology and financial services, along with the operational expertise and industry relationships needed to take Phase into its next stage of growth. As we bring our technology to market, she will lead the company’s commercial development and global expansion,” said Kirill Eves, founder of Phase.

Phase is a technology company building the operating layer for the AI agent economy, with four integrated services that give AI agents everything they need to operate autonomously, from accessing the open web and orchestrating AI models to performing computing tasks and making payments. The platform runs on its own Layer 1 blockchain, powered by a decentralized network of everyday devices. Phase has received $45 million in funding from its founder, Kirill Eves.

Phase Proxy enables AI agents acting on behalf of users to access websites that restrict automated traffic through mobile and residential internet connections. Phase Router intelligently directs requests across leading AI models to optimize quality, performance and cost. Phase Compute harnesses the processing power of devices across the network to run open-weight AI models, while on-chain settlement enables autonomous payments using stablecoins and PHASE, the network’s native token. Phase is building its own AI model to serve as the platform’s central intelligence, capable of advanced reasoning, solving complex tasks independently and orchestrating other AI models.

Unlike most blockchain networks that require dedicated servers or token staking, Phase allows anyone to become a validator simply by downloading the app, without specialized hardware or upfront investment. Its reputation-based consensus and randomized validator selection secure the network and prevent control from concentrating in the hands of a few powerful operators. Phase rewards device owners with PHASE tokens for validating blocks and contributing connectivity and computing power, enabling millions of people to help build the AI economy and share in the value it creates.

#5232. EU Assembles Task Force To Counter Russia

Home » Regulations » EU Assembles Task Force To Counter Russia

The EU announced two initiatives to bolster the bloc’s sanctions toolbox with enhanced global presence.

The European Union’s (EU) fresh crypto-focused task force is set to tackle top sanction evading challenges, mostly ascribed to Russia. Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque announced this to the public following the tenth meeting of the High-Level Expert Group on Union Restrictive Measures.

After the gathering in Brussels, this new EU regulatory arm aims to close gaps that allow Russia to sustain economic activity amid ongoing sanctions linked to its Ukraine invasion. The meeting brought together senior representatives from EU countries, the European Commission, and the External Action Service.

INTEL: EU sets up crypto task force to stop Russia dodging sanctions with digital assets

The examination of emerging financial threats revolves around crypto currency as a safe haven for tax or sanction evasion, keeping a strong commitment to Ukraine. Complementing the task force represents a broader dedicated sanctions office within the EU Commission. This improves coordination across member states.

The G7 is taking a more unified stance across policy, outreach & implementantion. It builds on 21 successive EU sanctions packages on Russia that have gradually targeted crypto-powered channels. Over the next 12 months, intelligence sharing and support from Ukraine and the UK will be used  to identify regular circumvention methods.

The latest sanction package, penned last Summer, freshly imposed transaction bans on 14 third country crypto platforms, enabling potential full bans on crypto services as well. By focusing on detection, enforcement consistency & international cooperation, the EU seeks to limit Russia’s ability to maintain economic resilience, still prevalent even after a flurry of sanction packages.

EU Launches Crypto Task Force to Crack Down on RussiaThe European Union has established a dedicated Crypto Sanctions Task Force to tackle sanctions evasion through digital assets.Announced on November 6, the program seeks to address the means through which Russia can evade… pic.twitter.com/uYJkWjr0Ez

Meanwhile, Russia recently implemented a new digital-asset focused law, lifting transaction & investment bans for retail customers that pass a special knowledgeability test. For businesses, the landscape has shifted too: Russian currency exchanges are able to legally offer crypto services from November 22, 2026, abiding by the legal framework from the local bank authority.

#5231. Ethereum – What BitMine’s $6.3B loss reveals about building treasury around ETH

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

The SEC has released BitMine’s Form 10-K.

According to the filing, the firm suffered a $6.3 billion net loss during the fiscal year ending August 31, 2026.

As the fiscal year runs from September 2025 to August 2026, the reported loss largely reflects Ethereum’s price decline following the October 2025 crash, which pushed ETH from a peak above $4k toward $2k.

In essence, much of the $6.3 billion loss came from unrealized losses on its ETH holdings.

The timing of the filing is also notable. BitMine has recently disclosed that it holds 6.07 million ETH, 216 BTC, and $475 million in cash and marketable securities. It also holds a stake in Beast Industries and Eightco. Altogether, its crypto, cash, securities, and moonshot investments were valued at $14.3 billion.

This demonstrates that the company has a large asset portfolio despite the large amount of paper loss they face. However, with ETH prices under pressure, continued accumulation also increases its exposure to further unrealized losses.

This brings attention to the recent thesis that Vitalik Buterin put forward regarding a new ‘store of value’ story. As previously covered by AMBCrypto, Buterin’s thesis aims to shift focus away from Ethereum’s deflationary model and instead focus on real demand for the asset.

Simply put, instead of relying mainly on reduced supply to drive value, the thesis puts greater emphasis on real demand and network adoption.

However, with BitMine alone losing $6.3 billion, it becomes an issue of whether the “demand-driven SOV” story holds when even the largest institutions holding ETH are losing significant sums.

This raises a key question: Does this put Ethereum’s long-term store-of-value narrative at risk?

For BitMine to get back into the green, Ethereum [ETH] would need a rally of nearly 50%.

However, the broader market signals suggest that recovery may not come easy. E

thereum has already underperformed Bitcoin by over 2x in Q4, falling nearly 25%. If the trend continues, the $2,000 level could come under pressure, pushing BitMine’s 6 million ETH holdings deeper into unrealized losses and adding more strain to its balance sheet.

Notably, the risk of holding such a large ETH position may also be starting to rise.

According to on-chain data, another 1,000 ETH worth $2.03 million was sold by one of the Ethereum Foundation’s wallets. Over the past week, large holders have sold a total of 17,800 ETH worth about $40 million. Meanwhile, BlackRock moved another $151 million worth of ETH to Coinbase Prime.

In essence, bulls are still not fully buying into Bitmine’s demand-driven SoV thesis.

Against this backdrop, Bitmine’s $6.3 billion in unrealized losses could put upward pressure on this scenario. As shown in the post above, BMNR is being seen by the market as a major catalyst for Ethereum becoming a SoV asset.

However, this narrative could face a reality check if ETH continues to underperform and Bitmine’s losses keep growing.

Thus, while BitMine’s 6 million ETH holdings suggest strong institutional demand, its recent SEC filing also demonstrates the dangers of such heavy accumulation, putting Ethereum’s long-term SoV story to the test.

BitMine’s $6.3 billion loss shows the risks of holding such a large amount of ETH as prices fall.

#5229. MSCI Confirms Strategy and Metaplanet Removal at November’s Rebalance

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: MSCI has confirmed that Strategy and Metaplanet will leave relevant equity indexes after the November 30 close. The change redirects benchmark-tracking funds’ shareholdings; it does not itself require either company to sell Bitcoin.

The uncertainty over whether MSCI would remove two prominent Bitcoin treasury companies has become a dated implementation event. Its November review places Strategy among US standard-index deletions and Metaplanet among Japanese small-cap deletions.

That gives investors a specific question to assess: how will demand for these companies’ shares change when funds following the affected benchmarks rebalance? It is a different question from whether the companies remain able or willing to hold Bitcoin.

MSCI’s standard-index changes name Strategy A in the US deletions column. Its small-cap changes list Metaplanet for removal in Japan. The provider’s review announcement, released November 11, says changes take effect after trading closes on November 30.

Investors therefore have a timetable rather than a consultation proposal. The distinction matters because a possible future exclusion and an announced rebalance can produce different positioning decisions, even if market participants have been preparing for the outcome.

For a fund whose mandate closely follows an affected index, holding an excluded stock may create a mismatch with that mandate. Other shareholders can make different decisions based on valuation and company strategy. That difference is why the rebalance identifies a channel of potential selling pressure without measuring the final market impact.

In its final methodology announcement, MSCI describes a first screen for substantial operating assets, followed by five financial ratios for companies that fail that initial test. Four flagged ratios can make a security ineligible, with timing rules intended to limit unnecessary turnover.

This is an index eligibility judgment. It should not be read as a determination that Bitcoin ownership is unlawful, or as a regulatory order to unwind a treasury. A benchmark provider decides what belongs in a particular investment universe; that decision can still carry significant commercial consequences for an excluded company.

Strategy’s consultation response argues that its Bitcoin activity is an operating business and criticizes MSCI’s approach. The company also says MSCI-linked funds held roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of basic shares outstanding, at the time of its response.

Those are Strategy’s estimates and arguments, not an independent forecast of the eventual selling. Current holdings, trading ahead of the rebalance and the methods individual funds use will affect how the change reaches the market. A holding estimate should not be presented as a guaranteed dollar outflow.

The potential connection runs through financing. If a treasury company can issue shares on attractive terms, it may use the proceeds to acquire Bitcoin. Less demand for those shares could make that route more expensive or less appealing. The outcome depends on valuation, alternative financing and management’s allocation decisions.

NewsBTC’s coverage of Strategy’s latest Bitcoin purchase and preferred-share repurchases shows why those choices need to be examined together. Raising capital does not mean every dollar automatically becomes a Bitcoin purchase.

The distinction also helps separate this event from redemptions in spot Bitcoin ETFs, which concern funds holding the asset itself. Selling a company’s stock changes its shareholder register; it does not directly transfer coins out of its treasury.

The next useful evidence will be the rebalance’s execution and subsequent financing disclosures. Until then, claims that the deletion guarantees a Bitcoin liquidation, or has no possible economic effect, both reach beyond what the announcement establishes.

#5227. Bitcoin ETFs Lose $299.8M as Five-Session Outflow Streak Reaches $1.44B

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $299.8 million in net outflows on November 11, the latest complete session in the data checked November 12. Five consecutive negative sessions now total approximately $1.44 billion. Individual funds are still moving in different directions.

Bitcoin’s US fund market has supplied another weak demand reading. The latest withdrawals extend a run in which new money entering some products has been insufficient to offset redemptions elsewhere.

The useful signal is the persistence of the imbalance. It deserves attention without turning one set of fund flows into a claim about every Bitcoin investor, or treating it as a reliable forecast of the next market move.

The Farside Investors table records a $269.7 million outflow from BlackRock’s IBIT and $39.1 million from Grayscale’s GBTC on November 11. Morgan Stanley’s MSBT received $9 million, leaving a $299.8 million net withdrawal across the tracked products.

Adding the table’s November 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11 net figures gives $1,437.9 million in withdrawals. That is a five-session total, with the intervening weekend excluded. November 12 entries were incomplete when checked and are not part of this calculation.

NewsBTC previously covered the November 9 ETF outflow. The new development is that two additional sessions have extended the negative run, rather than a revision that makes the earlier report a separate loss.

The positive MSBT reading prevents the session from being described accurately as a withdrawal from every product. Fund selection can reflect fees, distribution relationships, portfolio changes or investor preference; a daily table cannot establish which explanation drove a particular order.

Morgan Stanley’s launch announcement describes MSBT as a product seeking to track Bitcoin and sets out a 0.14% sponsor fee at launch. That product structure provides context for its place in the market. It does not prove that lower fees caused the latest inflow.

Nor does one fund’s gain cancel the broader imbalance. Investors can distinguish competitive shifts between providers from the total amount entering or leaving the group.

An ETF share can change hands on an exchange without the fund adding or removing underlying assets. Creation and redemption activity is the mechanism that changes the fund’s share count and asset base.

The IBIT prospectus available through iShares explains that authorized participants create and redeem baskets using cash or Bitcoin. That is why large exchange trading volume alone should not be mistaken for equally large new investment in the trust.

There is a related distinction between outflows and assets under management. A fund’s asset value can fall because Bitcoin declines, because investors redeem, or through both effects. Combining those changes without separating them can exaggerate the amount of investor withdrawal.

For traders, a continuing outflow streak may indicate that this particular source of demand remains under pressure. It still leaves open what is happening in direct spot markets, derivatives or corporate treasury accounts.

NewsBTC’s report on October inflation and the rate outlook provides another part of the market backdrop. The ETF figures alone do not establish that inflation, rates or any single headline caused the redemptions.

A sustained return to inflows would change the evidence. One positive session would be a narrower improvement. For now, the conclusion supported by the completed data is persistent net withdrawal from the tracked US spot funds, with an important exception at the individual-provider level.

#5225. Xash Brings Gold Rewards to Solana Stablecoin Users

Home » Altcoins » Solana (SOL) » Xash Brings Gold Rewards to Solana Stablecoin Users

The platform aims to tackle DeFi’s reliance on short-term incentives.

Xash, a Solana-based application that rewards users with tokenized gold for stablecoin activity, has announced its public launch at Solana Breakpoint 2026 in London, scheduled for November 15–17.

The platform aims to change how users earn rewards in decentralized finance (DeFi) by offering gold instead of temporary token incentives. Users can earn rewards by lending stablecoins, providing liquidity and trading across established Solana DeFi platforms.

The launch comes as DeFi protocols continue to face a challenge: attracting users who stay after promotional rewards expire. Xash is betting that gold-backed rewards could offer a more sustainable alternative.

Many DeFi platforms use token rewards to attract deposits and trading activity. However, users often move their funds elsewhere once those incentives end, creating a cycle known as mercenary capital.

Xash wants to address this problem by rewarding ongoing stablecoin activity with tokenized gold rather than short-lived token campaigns.

The company says the approach is intended to encourage longer-term participation in DeFi while giving users an opportunity to accumulate gold.

It also aims to benefit DeFi platforms seeking sustained activity and stablecoin issuers looking to expand the use of their tokens.

“Stablecoins don’t have a supply problem. They have a usage problem. Incentive campaigns rent users for a few weeks, then they’re gone,” said Kevin Huynh, co-founder and CEO of Xash.

Xash aggregates DeFi opportunities into a single interface, evaluating available strategies daily and presenting users with options based on potential gold rewards.

Before committing funds, users can review associated costs and estimated 30-day rewards. They can then select an opportunity and authorize transactions directly through their own wallets.

As part of the launch, the company is introducing direct withdrawals of accumulated tokenized gold rewards to users’ wallets. It is also adding a curated liquidity vault built on Kamino, allowing users to deploy stablecoins through a single deposit instead of managing individual transactions.

Xash says its trading activity does not involve directional price bets or borrowed funds. However, this does not eliminate the risks associated with DeFi. Users remain exposed to the underlying protocols and market conditions, including potential losses when using the Kamino vault.

The project was founded by Kevin Huynh, who serves as CEO, alongside Vinny Lingham, co-founder of Civic and Gyft and a former general partner at Multicoin Capital; Alen Ribic, co-founder of SweepSouth; and Llew Claasen, former executive director of the Bitcoin Foundation.

Xash’s launch comes amid growing demand for tokenized real-world assets (RWAs), particularly gold-backed digital tokens.

According to the World Gold Council, the tokenized gold market has expanded fivefold since late 2024, reaching approximately $6 billion.

Trading activity has also accelerated. Tokenized gold generated more than $90 billion in spot trading volume during the first quarter of 2026 alone, surpassing the total recorded throughout 2025, according to CoinGecko research.

Xash tests whether real-asset rewards can retain DeFi users better than short-term token incentives. Its launch also reflects rising demand for tokenized gold within the Solana ecosystem.

#5222. ‘Do not let Sauron have the ring’: Voorhees warns against a government veto on AI

His Sauron warning targets control over AI releases, a power already proposed in a September bill and El-Sayed’s campaign platform.

“Do not let Sauron have the ring,” Erik Voorhees, founder of AI service Venice, wrote on Nov. 12, warning against giving politicians control over artificial intelligence. His post as @ErikVoorhees targeted the concentration of political power over machine intelligence.

His warning followed a clip of All-In co-host David Sacks predicting a Democratic push for a federal department to approve frontier AI models before release. A September Sanders-Casar bill already proposes such a department and approval powers for covered advanced AI systems. El-Sayed's October Senate campaign platform proposes an agency that could block releases, with a different set of safeguards.

The clip published by @firesidealpha on Nov. 7 shows Sacks predicting a major Democratic push for AI legislation in the next Congress. He describes a federal AI department reviewing the most advanced models, giving developers its concerns and withholding release until those concerns are addressed.

Sacks goes further, alleging that Democrats want AI-powered surveillance and censorship. The proposals establish release-blocking powers, not the political motives he alleges.

The remarks came from the Nov. 7 All-In episode, announced by @theallinpod. In the full episode, Sacks also predicts a bargain in which government gains more power while closed-model companies gain regulatory protection. His concern therefore reaches beyond censorship to the possibility that compliance rules could protect established developers from competition.

Voorhees argues that open-source transparency and decentralization provide better safety, and that licensing undermines equality. His objection is to anyone holding that gatekeeping power.

Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on Sept. 23, before Sacks's November remarks. The introduced Senate version, S.5493, would establish a Department of Artificial Intelligence, pause advanced AI development pending a regulatory framework and prohibit artificial superintelligence.

Its proposed approval mechanism is explicit. Section 9(d) would prevent a person from deploying, releasing, importing or transferring an advanced AI system before receiving the department's approval. The secretary would inspect for characteristics posing a danger to the public, including superintelligence and precursor characteristics, and withhold approval if dangerous characteristics are present.

The bill would also require a charter to develop or distribute advanced AI. Maintaining that charter would entail giving regulators access to systems, processes, staff and physical infrastructure. Separate provisions would require pauses and shutdown measures for specified dangerous systems.

This would put a federal decision between a covered developer and release of its model. It resembles the institutional mechanism Sacks describes much more closely than a voluntary testing arrangement does. It remains proposed legislation, however, rather than evidence that the next Congress has agreed to create such a system.

The bill also contains constraints on the regulator. It proposes Senate confirmation of the secretary, independent scientific advice and employee financial-interest restrictions. It provides Federal Circuit review of findings underlying charter revocations. That specific remedy is not a general appeal of every model-release decision.

Abdul El-Sayed's Oct. 13 “AI Under Control” platform calls for an independent, Cabinet-level agency empowered to inspect laboratories, block releases, order pauses and command shutdowns. The campaign document explicitly builds on the Sanders-Casar legislation.

It proposes freezing training and release of the most powerful systems until safety rules and enforcement exist, with independent scientists certifying safety before the pause lifts. It also calls for independent pre-release audits and mandatory breach reporting to government within 24 hours, accompanied by public summaries.

The safeguards are part of the proposal, too. A scientific board chosen outside the agency would manage its governance. Exemptions would be public, industry fees would fund the regulator and officials would be barred from later cashing in on the companies they regulate. The platform also supports whistleblower protections and preserving stronger state laws.

Crucially for Sacks's surveillance allegation, the document reiterates opposition to warrantless surveillance. Its stated prohibitions also include autonomous weapons firing and replacing human oversight in life-or-death decisions. The proposed release powers do not establish Sacks's allegation about the purpose they would serve.

Those protections do not eliminate the concentration of authority Voorhees opposes. An agency able to stop a release would retain that power even with outside scientific oversight. The safeguards seek to constrain its use, while leaving the regulator with a veto over covered releases.

The platform does not set out a detailed release-approval or appeal procedure. Its outside-selected scientific board also differs from S.5493's advisory board, whose members the secretary would select. The two proposals overlap in coercive powers while making different choices about who advises or governs the regulator.

Introduced legislation: Senate confirmation, scientific advice, financial restrictions and review of charter-revocation findings.

Campaign proposal: an outside-selected scientific board, public exemptions and limits on officials profiting from regulated companies.

Release-blocking powers are already proposed. The bill and campaign platform put different safeguards around that authority.

Both are proposals, not an enacted common system. S.5493 covers defined advanced AI. The Federal Circuit route shown concerns findings behind charter revocations, not general release-approval appeals. The campaign platform does not detail an approval or appeal procedure.

Sacks's reference to the next Congress comes against an election shift. CryptoSlate, citing Associated Press, reported that Democrats had won the House and unified control of Congress in its election coverage, updated Nov. 8.

Existing federal policy also needs to be distinguished from the proposed approval regime. Trump's June 2 executive order directs a voluntary framework for government access to frontier models. Section 3(c) expressly says that section does not authorize mandatory government licensing, preclearance or permitting for new models. That limitation concerns the framework in that order, rather than every other government power over AI.

For Voorhees, the issue is longstanding and tied to his business. His July 2024 introduction to Venice identifies him as founder and CEO, describes an application using leading open-source models and argues against corporate or government monopoly over intelligence. CryptoSlate also covered the connection between model-access restrictions and decentralized AI in June.

The next legislative test is whether these proposals gain committee action and leadership backing, and what any new text says about release criteria, decision-making authority and review of adverse decisions.

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

TL;DR: Canaan’s results put hardware sales, treasury assets and a newly announced share-buyback program under scrutiny. Operating performance and accounting gains tell different stories.

Canaan’s quarter calls for a closer look at which activities generate cash, which change reported earnings and which consume accumulated capital. A share repurchase, an equipment sale and a change in Bitcoin’s valuation can each affect shareholders through a different route.

For investors, the practical task is to follow three different activities: selling mining equipment, operating miners and managing accumulated digital assets. Each contributes to the company’s economics in a different way.

In its November 10 earnings release, Canaan reported $4.8 million in products revenue, versus $118.6 million a year earlier. Total revenue fell from $150.5 million to $14.5 million. The company attributed the equipment decline to lower computing power sold and weaker selling prices.

That combination matters. Selling fewer units affects scale, while lower prices can squeeze the amount available to cover development and overhead. A recovery in demand would therefore need to be assessed alongside margins, rather than judged solely by the number of machines shipped.

Canaan reported $8 million in net income alongside a $42.9 million operating loss. Its financial tables separately identify gains from cryptocurrency revaluation and financial derivatives. Those items help explain why the bottom line and the operating result point in different directions.

A rising value for assets already held can improve reported earnings without creating a matching amount of new cash. Equally, selling part of a reserve can generate cash while reducing future exposure to the asset. Neither observation makes the accounting result invalid; they explain why it is incomplete as a measure of trading health.

The contrast between revenue, backlog and losses at Bitdeer is another example of why mining-related companies need more than a headline earnings comparison.

Canaan’s September operating update, issued October 15, said it had monetized 3,952 ETH and 54.5 BTC for approximately $13.9 million. It also described repurchases funded through its existing program. Those sales were previously disclosed activity, not a new November transaction.

The latest release adds an initial $20 million repurchase program under a $100 million board authorization. Authorization gives management permission to act; it should not be confused with completed purchases of that amount.

Buying back shares and retaining Bitcoin involve competing uses of capital. A repurchase may benefit remaining holders if the price and funding choices are attractive, but it also uses resources that could support equipment development, liquidity or infrastructure. The decision needs to be judged on those terms, rather than treated as automatically bullish for either asset.

The company’s second-quarter report had already described reducing inventory, matching production to demand and preserving financial flexibility. It reported $31.9 million in revenue for that earlier period, showing that the latest result follows an existing slowdown.

NewsBTC’s account of MARA selling Bitcoin while developing AI infrastructure provides a related capital-allocation comparison, though the companies’ operating models differ.

The next useful checkpoints are cash generated by operations, actual repurchases and disclosed project commitments. A larger infrastructure ambition or an improved crypto valuation can change the investment story, but neither by itself demonstrates that demand for Canaan’s core products has recovered.

#5219. Ripple’s Bank-Style Lending on XRPL Nears Launch: What XRP Holders Actually Get

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has collected 22 of 35 votes (62.86%).

Three more validators have signed on over the past three weeks. Ripple's own nodes have already voted yes, along with the University of Waterloo and UC Berkeley.

To go live, the amendment has to clear the 80% bar (29 votes) and hold it for two straight weeks.

The related SingleAssetVault amendment (XLS-65) has 23 votes (65.7%) and needs six more.

The XLS-65 and XLS-66 standards drop overcollateralization and instant liquidations and let companies take out fixed-term, uncollateralized loans directly on XRPL. The loans work similarly to traditional bank credit, with a fixed term and pre-set interest terms.

Ripple has already tested the protocol on a private XRPL network with nine nodes that matched the hardware of its mainnet nodes.

Holders deposit XRP or stablecoins such as RLUSD into Single Asset Vaults and receive shares. Interest is paid on a cash basis. Depositors receive it only after the borrower has sent the money. Withdrawals from a vault are processed on a first-come, first-served basis.

Borrowers are vetted off-chain by Loan Brokers, who record each disbursement on the ledger. According to the XRPL documentation, the protocol "relies on off-chain underwriting and risk management to assess the creditworthiness of borrowers."

The broker's own "first-loss capital" covers losses first when a client stops paying.

Issuers can also freeze assets or claw them back. According to Ripple, all operations in a vault and in the connected lending protocol stop when an asset issuer freezes the vault.

Until now, XRP holders who wanted passive income had to use third-party bridges and wrapped tokens. After the amendment activates, holders can deposit XRP in a pool on XRPL, with its fraction-of-a-cent fees, and collect part of the interest paid by borrowers. Their income will depend on the terms set by the loan broker and on borrowers' repayments.

If a major borrower defaults and the broker's first-loss capital runs out, depositors bear the losses and their shares drop in value.

#5218. Hyperscale Data Sells Remaining Bitcoin Reserve to Fund Michigan AI Buildout

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Hyperscale Data says it sold its remaining Bitcoin reserves by November 8, raising about $16 million from the final sale. The money is intended for debt reduction and its Michigan AI campus. Its Montana Bitcoin mining operation continues.

A Bitcoin reserve can serve as a long-term investment, a source of emergency liquidity or funding for a different business. Hyperscale Data has made its current preference clear: accumulated coins are being converted into capital for infrastructure and debt repayment.

The decision shifts the investment question toward execution. Shareholders now need to evaluate what the company can earn from the projects it funds, alongside the Bitcoin exposure it has given up.

In its November 10 announcement, Hyperscale Data said the final disposal involved approximately 211.56 BTC at around $76,000 per coin. Since sales began in late July, it said it had sold roughly 1,113 BTC for approximately $74.4 million.

The reported proceeds are cash raised from sales, not a statement of trading profit. Calculating a realized gain or loss would require the relevant cost basis and accounting treatment. Multiplying a sale price by the coins sold cannot answer that question.

The company expects future balance-sheet Bitcoin to come mainly from mining. That makes the November 8 reserve snapshot different from a promise never to hold Bitcoin again.

Management is targeting December for the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity to be energized. That is a target, with construction and commissioning still relevant to whether it is achieved.

The funding effort extends beyond the crypto sales. An October 28 company release described hiring Newmark to seek long-term debt financing for the campus. It explicitly said the engagement was not a lending commitment and that financing terms had not been announced.

That distinction is important when assessing liquidity. Hiring an adviser may improve access to prospective lenders, but only completed financing provides committed capital on agreed terms. Interest costs, collateral and repayment schedules would also influence the eventual economics.

The October financing update describes an initial 20-MW customer arrangement with a ten-year term and extension options. Additional capacity and longer duration depend on the applicable contractual conditions.

Earlier, in a September development update, Hyperscale Data said it had invested more than $70 million in Alliance Cloud Services and the Michigan facility. That historical spending helps explain the project’s capital intensity; it does not establish how much remains to be funded or what return the investment will earn.

For an infrastructure business, the progression from agreement to energized capacity and customer billing matters more than the largest possible contract headline. Optional expansion should not be added to near-term revenue as though it were already delivered.

NewsBTC has reported similar capital-allocation choices at MARA and Riot Platforms. The comparison is that coins can finance a new operating strategy; the companies’ projects and balance sheets should still be assessed separately.

An individual reserve sale cannot establish that all miners are abandoning Bitcoin, especially where mining continues. It can, however, change what shareholders are effectively backing: less accumulated digital-asset exposure and more reliance on future business cash flows.

For Hyperscale Data, evidence of funded construction, completed commissioning and actual customer revenue would make that transition easier to evaluate. The reserve disposal supplies capital. Whether the new use of it creates more value remains an operating question.

#5217. Finland Turns Bitcoin Miners Into Discounted Home-Heating

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » Finland Turns Bitcoin Miners Into Discounted Home-Heating

In the town of Nokia, Finland, a 180-square-meter house now relies entirely on Bitcoin mining rigs for warmth.

During the frigid months of winter in Northern Europe, heating efficiency is the main topic of discussion even in the richest neighborhoods. The frequently hostile surroundings have urged heating specialists to come up with new, creative ways to replace traditional oil heating with cutting-edge technology.

That’s where Bitcoin (BTC) comes into play: Finnish homes have already adapted liquid-cooled mining machine heaters. They utilize the gains equipped from Bitcoin (BTC) mining venues to offset the costs of heating. On the other hand, that kind of solution is highly-dependent on the hash-rate difficulty across the network, among factors like general market conditions.

The next BTC block-reward halving comes in 2028, which could arguably cap the profits of this kind of business if Bitcoin (BTC) crosses $135,000. With installation costs exceeding $20,000, SunBit’s Bitcoin Boiler is aimed at relieving high-heating costs for the residents of Finland. The machine is supposed to work in-profit as long as Bitcoin’s price stays above $70,000.

Some people use Bitcoin mining to make money.In Finland, people are using it to heat their homes.A Finnish startup called SunBit has installed Bitcoin mining machines that double as home heating systems.The concept is pretty wild.Instead of letting the heat generated by… pic.twitter.com/9S4hqTYSl6

For instance, in a historical house in Tampere, Finland’s third-largest city, mining rigs replaced wood burning, maintaining a 1,500-liter water tank between 50°C and 60°C. Sunbit’s liquid-cooled Bitcoin miner utilizes the Antminer S21 XP Hydro, employing a hash rate of up to 495T. The device consumes 5.3 kilowatts of power & draws about 46,400 kWh annually.

The Bitcoin Boiler device stores this heat in water, reaching temperatures up to 60 degrees Celsius, which is then circulated throughout the house via radiators and underfloor heating pipes. It costs roughly $5,200 a year to run. SunBit founder Elmeri Suomi stated: “The heating function itself is unaffected by market conditions; only the payback period changes.”

🇫🇮 🔥 Underground Bitcoin mining in Finland is used to heat its towns, instead of being wasted. pic.twitter.com/EHOfxcWq6M

Bitcoin-based heating systems have first been tested in the Netherlands, but Finland’s adoption mark has grown way further. The Bitcoin Boiler service fee is optional and includes 24/7 remote monitoring with automatic heating strategy optimization aligned with Finland’s floating electricity prices. This runs in a companion app with grid peak-shaving options for advanced enthusiasts.

Amid ongoing volatility, can Bitcoin bulls prevent a pullback toward $60k?

The most recent CPI release has caused a strong risk-off move and pushed BTC down below $75k. While it is still only 4% from November open, the risk of further downside is increasing.

Technically, $75k is an important level, as it is a cost basis for short-term holders, meaning it could form a significant supply zone, with investors looking to sell at close to breakeven.

The recent Glassnode report adds another layer. As can be seen in the chart below, the largest Bitcoin liquidity cluster is concentrated around $60k. These are mostly longs opened at the bottom of the market, which haven’t been re-tested by BTC since it rallied from around $65k in August.

$60k is therefore a major downside liquidity cluster that is around 20% away from $75k.

The key takeaway? According to Glassnode analysts, a rally to $60k could result in large amounts of long-term liquidation. However, this can create an accumulation opportunity for patient accumulators, those who are looking to take advantage of the forced selling.

This certainly adds pressure at the $75k level. Technically, Bitcoin is still inside this range, and there isn’t much to lose here for bulls. But with how the recent CPI data has gone, it might be harder to stay above $75k.

The expectations for December rate cuts have changed, and the on-chain fundamentals are very bearish.

So, if there is not enough buy-side liquidity to absorb the sell-side liquidity around $75k, BTC could face a deeper correction as long liquidations accelerate. This could bring the $60k liquidity pocket into focus, where even bullish investors may find a better accumulation opportunity.

The broader liquidity crunch is now weighing on the Bitcoin network.

The result? As can be seen in the chart below, Bitcoin’s daily trading volume has dropped to a record low of 126k BTC in 2026. This is down from around 453k BTC in 2022. So, technically, there has been an overall decline of around 72% in Bitcoin’s spot trading volume.

The key takeaway? Glassnode says a return to supply growth would be the first sign that new money is coming in.

In essence, the decline in stablecoin and Spot volumes shows that there is more liquidity being drained from the market. This will leave Bitcoin much more vulnerable and will make it harder to hold the $75k level. In turn, the $60k region is looking like an area of accumulation, reinforcing Glassnode’s thesis.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, sending the chipmaker's shares tumbling and intensifying a selloff across cryptocurrency markets.

On Nov. 12, the company announced that Huang had stepped down as chief executive, president, and board member, effective immediately, ending his 33-year leadership of the artificial intelligence giant.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent replacement. Harvey Jones, a longtime director and former Synopsys executive, will serve as board chairman.

The company did not specify a reason for Huang's resignation.

However, the departure had followed reports of Huang's extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected by US authorities of having Chinese intelligence connections. Nvidia's board had launched an independent investigation into the allegations, which remain unproven.

The upheaval triggered a sharp decline in Nvidia shares, which fell as much as 10% in premarket trading to approximately $156.

At that price, the company's implied market capitalization would fall to roughly $3.8 trillion, nearly $2 trillion below its October peak of approximately $5.8 trillion.

Speaking on this performance, CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju noted that:

“[Nvidia stock's] analyst sentiment just hit -2.6σ, the most bearish on record.”

The selling extended to Nvidia-backed AI infrastructure companies. CoreWeave fell more than 13% in premarket trading, while Nebius declined about 20% amid concerns about its growth outlook.

The uncertainty also spilled into cryptocurrency markets, where Bitcoin and Ethereum fell to their lowest price values since August. BTC fell below $71,500, while ETH dropped below $1,990, per CryptoSlate data.

The market reaction reflects Nvidia's central role in the AI investment boom, with Huang overseeing both its dominance in advanced processors and an expanding network of financial arrangements supporting companies that buy them.

The leadership crisis has also revived concerns about Nvidia's role in financing the AI infrastructure expansion, particularly the circular investment arrangements connecting chip suppliers, cloud operators and AI developers.

Nic Puckrin, chief executive of Coin Bureau, warned that replacing Huang could backfire on the broader AI industry, citing his central role in negotiating financing agreements.

Puckrin questioned whether a successor could replicate those arrangements and whether uncertainty over Nvidia's direction could undermine confidence in the sector's investment model.

The concerns come amid growing scrutiny of circular financing, with AI companies increasingly funding businesses that also purchase their products and services.

An October study by the Bank for International Settlements found that 55.2% of incoming investment value in AI companies between 2021 and 2025 came from other AI businesses.

Of that AI-to-AI investment value, 46.4% involved companies that also maintained commercial relationships with recipients, equivalent to approximately 25.6% of overall incoming investment value.

Nvidia is among the companies participating in such arrangements. In January, the chipmaker invested $2 billion in CoreWeave, a cloud infrastructure provider that purchases Nvidia processors.

The investment accompanied an agreement to accelerate CoreWeave's development of AI data centers, deepening the financial relationship between Nvidia and one of its major customers.

The arrangements have drawn comparisons to the late-1990s telecommunications boom, when equipment manufacturers financed network operators' purchases of their products. The subsequent collapse in demand exposed suppliers to declining sales and losses on their financing commitments.

Huang's resignation does not alter Nvidia's existing contracts. However, his successor will inherit an increasingly interconnected investment network whose sustainability depends on continued growth in demand for AI computing.

Nvidia's Nov. 17 earnings call will give investors a chance to assess whether the leadership transition changes its approach to financing customers and supporting infrastructure expansion.

TL;DR: Fold reported $4.2 million in third-quarter revenue and a $2.6 million net loss. The company says Bitcoin gift-card sales helped lift custody and trading revenue, while newer products aim to encourage customers to keep balances on its platform.

Selling someone their first Bitcoin product is one commercial challenge. Giving them enough reasons to keep using the same financial app is another. Fold’s latest results show a company trying to connect those two activities.

That approach could create a more durable customer relationship, but its economics depend on retention and the cost of rewards. New accounts, product launches and transaction volume are useful indicators; they are not interchangeable with profit.

In its November 10 quarterly announcement, Fold said TikTok Shop had become its largest gift-card and customer-acquisition channel. It attributed an approximate 270% increase in custody and trading revenue to gift-card sales.

This is the company’s description of the channel’s performance, rather than evidence that every gift-card recipient becomes a recurring customer. The distinction is commercially important: a promotional purchase can generate revenue once, while a lasting relationship may support repeat activity.

Fold’s explanation of its rewards model says eligible spending earns actual Bitcoin that can be retained or withdrawn. That makes the product easier to understand than a reward that first requires conversion from a proprietary points system. It also leaves the dollar value of the reward exposed to Bitcoin’s price after it is received.

Fold also reported more than 88,500 verified accounts and approximately 2,500 early-access credit-card holders. Management is emphasizing customer balances alongside transactions following the launch of Fold Reserve and Lead Bank spending accounts.

For a financial platform, retained balances can create opportunities for recurring revenue and broader product use. The relevant follow-up is whether that opportunity exceeds the cost of acquiring customers, servicing accounts and funding incentives. A larger account base alone does not answer it.

NewsBTC’s report on BitPay adding familiar mobile checkout options examines another attempt to reduce friction around crypto purchases. Easier entry and lasting engagement are related goals, with different measures of success.

Fold’s Reserve product page describes Reserve as stored value rather than an FDIC-insured deposit account. The balance determines access to reward tiers; it does not itself earn interest. The page also explains that advertised rewards depend on conditions such as qualifying balances and eligible spending.

That distinction matters when a company discusses gathering customer assets. A spending account at a partner bank, a stored-value balance and Bitcoin custody may sit inside one app while carrying different terms and protections. Product presentation should not blur them into a single type of savings account.

The company’s Bitcoin help page identifies BitGo as its Bitcoin custodian and says Bitcoin purchases and rewards do not receive FDIC or SIPC protection. NewsBTC’s recent look at BitGo’s results provides background on that infrastructure provider.

Fold’s adjusted EBITDA was a $4.5 million loss, compared with a $5.5 million loss in the preceding quarter. That improvement is relevant, but it remains a negative adjusted result and should be considered alongside the reported net loss.

The strongest future evidence would connect customer acquisition to retained balances, sustained activity and better unit economics. Investors should also watch whether incentives remain commercially affordable as the products grow.

The latest update identifies promising distribution and engagement experiments. It leaves the central question open: can Fold turn easier access to Bitcoin rewards into a consistently profitable financial-services relationship?

None of these uncertainties change the underlying architectural advantage: the Layer 1 can remain a focused means of exchange while the surrounding ecosystem gains the capacity for richer functionality.

#5211. Onramp Launches Business Bitcoin Accounts With Team Withdrawal Approvals

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Onramp has launched a business Bitcoin account with named users, role permissions and withdrawal approvals. A separate Treasury tier adds multi-institution custody. The distinction matters because team account controls and the underlying signing arrangement are different parts of security.

For a company buying Bitcoin, the first operational question arrives quickly: who is allowed to move it? A purchase approved by the board still needs a process for everyday access, record keeping and changes in personnel.

Onramp’s new offering addresses that administrative layer. Its significance is practical: making a corporate Bitcoin position something a finance team can govern through defined responsibilities, rather than treating account access as one person’s private task.

The company’s November 10 announcement says Onramp Business supports up to three named users, role-based permissions, withdrawal approval policies and an audit trail. The entry account has no monthly charge and a stated 0.85% trading fee, with assets held by a qualified custodian.

Those features are intended to separate initiating a payment from authorizing it. In a well-designed company process, the person preparing a transfer need not have unilateral authority to complete it. An audit trail can then help explain who requested and approved an action if it is later questioned.

That does not remove the need for an internal policy. A system can enforce permissions only after the business decides who should have them, which transfers require review and what happens when an employee leaves.

Onramp’s current product page lists its Treasury tier from $375 a month, with a 0.65% trading fee. It includes vaults in the company’s name and a structure requiring two of three institutions to move Bitcoin. The page labels custom approval rules as forthcoming.

The basic account should therefore not be described as already including every Treasury feature. Likewise, a planned feature should not appear in a list of capabilities customers can use today.

Separating those tiers also makes pricing easier to interpret. A monthly service charge and a trading fee pay for different things; the cost comparison depends on the amount held, transaction frequency and the control arrangements a company actually needs.

Bitcoin.org’s wallet-security guidance explains that multisignature arrangements can require several independent signatures before funds move. The general idea is to make compromise of one device or authority insufficient to authorize a transaction.

Operational approvals in an application and cryptographic signatures are not automatically the same safeguard. A finance team needs to understand both: what its own users can approve, and which parties ultimately control the keys needed to spend the assets.

NewsBTC has covered related approaches through Sygnum’s shared-key Bitcoin lending arrangement and AnchorWatch’s custody and insurance offering. Those services address different use cases, but each makes the allocation of control central to the product.

The less visible test is what happens when normal operations break down. A director may leave, an authorized employee may become unavailable, or a service provider may be unable to complete its part. A company considering custody needs a documented recovery process as well as a normal withdrawal process.

Extra checks can introduce friction, so a treasury also needs to distinguish assets reserved for long-term holding from assets it may need to move quickly. Strong controls are most useful when they fit the business’s actual payment and liquidity requirements.

Onramp’s launch offers another route for putting those responsibilities into a managed service. Whether it suits a particular company depends on the contractual terms, key structure, costs and operating requirements, rather than the existence of a Bitcoin account alone.
